Damage + Property: Read Any House

Welcome back. She has been winterized, cleared, and inspected — and time has still had its way with her. Today the class walks back inside and learns to read her the way a doctor reads a patient: what is wrong, where it is, and how bad it is.

That passcode doesn't open this door. Try again.

Chapter 1 · From memory

No notes. Winterize her — then do the maths.

Before anything new, we go back — from memory alone. Last class the class learned winterization by heart, and learned to measure a debris pile honestly. If they can still say both, they walk into today carrying tools. If they can't, today has nothing to stand on.

Keep those in your pocket. Today we walk back into our house after time away — and learn to read her.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1, and she is never named again. If this is a new group, or the name needs saying out loud to bring her back — here it is. Pick the name the class chose, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, eighth chapter.

First, prove the maths is still yours

A debris pile, measured in feet. Length × width × height gives cubic feet — divide by 27 and you have honest cubic yards. Try the pile from last class first: 9 × 6 × 3. Then try any pile of your own.

Say it in class

“Close your notes. Winterize her for me, step by step — and then: a pile nine feet by six by three. How many honest cubic yards? And what happens to a bill that claims fifteen?”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Quick way back in: water left sitting in pipes freezes, expands, and bursts them — so before a cold season, the house's water is made safe. The water is shut off at the main. Every line is drained empty. Antifreeze goes into every trap and every toilet, so the little pools of water that can't drain don't freeze and crack the porcelain. The water heater is handled exactly as the order states — no improvising. A notice is posted so the next person through the door knows the house is winterized. And the whole thing is photographed: the meter, the shutoff, and each fixture, so the work can be proved later.

The steps, in the order they happen

  1. Shut the water off at the main.
  2. Drain every line.
  3. Antifreeze in every trap and every toilet.
  4. The water heater — exactly as the order states.
  5. Post the notice.
  6. Photograph the meter, the shutoff, and each fixture.

If you've done this work before

You already know the two traps this recall is really testing. First: a missing fixture photo means the file comes back — the proof is part of the job, not paperwork after it. Second: if the system won't hold pressure or a valve is stuck, the honest move is HOLD and report. A failed test is information, not failure — and faking one is how a small job becomes the most expensive damage in the house.

The line to remember: “The cheapest job that prevents the most expensive damage.”

The proof — what “done” has to show

Here's what a winterization has to be able to prove, so the recall never rests on memory alone.

Every trapAntifreeze in each one — one missed trap is one cracked fixture waiting for January
Each fixturePhotographed — meter, shutoff, and every fixture, or the file comes back
As orderedThe water heater handled exactly as the order states — the order's rulebook governs, always

If this is all new to you

Debris is measured in cubic yards — the amount of space a pile takes up. Measure the pile in feet: length times width times height gives you cubic feet. One cubic yard holds 27 cubic feet, so you divide by 27. The pile from last class: 9 × 6 × 3 = 162 cubic feet, and 162 ÷ 27 = 6 cubic yards. If a bill claims 15 yards for that same pile, the bill is claiming two and a half piles that don't exist. The maths catches it in ten seconds.

How the check runs, step by step

  1. Measure the pile: length, width, height — in feet.
  2. Multiply the three numbers: that's cubic feet.
  3. Divide by 27: that's cubic yards.
  4. Hold the bill next to the answer. If they don't match, the bill — not the maths — has to explain itself.

If you've done this work before

Notice why this maths opens a class about reading a house: quantifying is the third step of today's skill, and this is the version of it the class already owns. A judgment without a number is a guess; a judgment with a number is a case. Today they learn to put numbers on damage the way they already put them on debris.

The line to remember: “Debris is where honesty is measured — literally.”

The proof — the arithmetic itself

162 cu ft9 × 6 × 3 feet — the pile from last class
6 CY162 ÷ 27 — the honest measure of that pile
15 CY ✗A bill for 15 yards on that pile fails the maths — send it back

The calculator above this drawer runs the same arithmetic on any pile the class names — it stores nothing and invents nothing.

Chapter 2 · The shape of today

Today we learn to read her.

We walk into our house after time away, and we learn to read her the way a doctor reads a patient: what is wrong, where it is, and how bad it is. Not fixing — not yet. Reading.

Two halves today, in this order: first the damage story — what happens to a house. Then the damage skill — how you judge it. Story first, skill second, because you cannot judge what you do not understand.

Say it in class

“Today we walk into our house after time away, and we learn to read her the way a doctor reads a patient: what is wrong, where it is, and how bad it is.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A doctor never starts with the cure. She looks, she listens, she asks where it hurts and how long it's been hurting — and only then does she name what's wrong. A house rewards the same patience. Walk in already reaching for the fix and you'll paint over stains that are still leaking, scrub mould that is still growing, and price jobs you haven't understood. Today is about the looking. The fixing belongs to other classes — and to people who read the house first.

How today is built, step by step

  1. Chapters 3 to 7: the damage story — five kinds of damage, one room at a time.
  2. Chapter 8: all five held in one table, the way you'll hold them on a real walk.
  3. Chapters 9 and 10: the house herself — her five systems, her age, her place, her season.
  4. Chapters 11 and 12: the skill — identify, document, quantify — and the decision that ends every reading: what does she need first?

If you've done this work before

You already live this order on good days: the inspection class taught that a report is a product — “an inspection does not fix anything; it tells the truth about everything.” Today generalises that line to every job. The reading habit is what makes the proof believable and the invoice defensible, because a number traced back to a named, measured, photographed fact is very hard to argue with.

The line to remember: “Read the house before you price the job.”

The proof — what this class will and won't claim

An honest note before the walk begins: the five damage kinds, the five systems, and the safety list on this page are the programme's working knowledge, taught the way the schedule carries them. The house-age figures in Chapter 10 come from published counts and name their source in that drawer. The three practice cases in Chapter 11 are teaching cases, written for this class and labelled as such — no real house, no real file, no real photograph stands behind them.

If this is all new to you

“Damage” sounds like one word. It isn't. Water seeps. Mold grows. People break. Weather strikes from outside. Neglect accumulates from inside time itself. Each kind leaves different signs when you walk in, and — this is the part that matters — each one points at a different next job. Learn to tell them apart and a strange house starts reading like a familiar sentence. Confuse them, and every job you plan starts from the wrong place.

How the walk runs, step by step

  1. We take the five kinds one at a time — a chapter each, a room each.
  2. For every kind: what it does, what it looks like when you walk in, and what it means for the next job.
  3. Then we lay all five side by side in one table (Chapter 8), because real houses never present one kind at a time.

If you've done this work before

The five kinds map straight onto the decisions you already make. Water decides whether a cosmetic scope is honest. Mold decides whether the moisture conversation happens before any cleaning scope. Vandalism decides whether the secure comes first. Weather decides whether the envelope is checked before interior work is promised. Neglect decides your expectations before you open the door: layered damage, more than one thing wrong, budget your attention accordingly.

The line to remember: “Five kinds — and each one is a different sentence about what happens next.”

The proof — the five, on one line each

WaterStains, swelling, soft floors → find the source before any cosmetic fix.
MoldDark spots + damp smell → moisture is still present; don't just paint over it.
VandalismBroken entries, stripped fixtures, graffiti → secure first, then assess.
WeatherRoof, wind, hail, ice marks → check roof + envelope before interior work.
NeglectOvergrowth, rot, pest signs → long vacancy; expect layered damage.
Chapter 3 · Damage, room one

Water is the quietest destroyer.

Water does not announce itself. You walk in and you see stains on a wall or a ceiling — brown rings where water has dried. You feel a floor that swells under your foot, or goes soft where it should be firm.

Water means one thing before anything else: find the source before any cosmetic fix.

Say it in class

“Painting over a water stain without finding the leak is like painting over a wound without stopping the bleeding. The stain comes back — and the damage underneath keeps growing.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Water writes in three ways. Stains: brown rings on a ceiling or wall, each ring a place where water pooled, spread, and dried — sometimes more than once. Swelling: wood and board drink water and puff up, so doors stick, boards lift, and surfaces that should be flat aren't. Softness: a floor that gives under your foot where it should be firm — the structure itself has been wet long enough to weaken. Train your eyes on the ceiling first: in a house, the stain is often one room away — and one floor below — the leak that made it.

How to read a water sign, step by step

  1. Name the sign out loud: stain, swelling, or soft floor — and the room it's in.
  2. Look up and look above: what sits over this spot — a roof, a bathroom, a pipe run?
  3. Ask the only question that matters at this stage: is it old and dry, or is the source still feeding it?
  4. Write down what you found exactly as found. The fix decision comes later; the reading is now.

If you've done this work before

Two field habits hide inside this chapter. First, “cosmetic” is a technical word here: paint, plaster, pretty finishes — surface beauty. A cosmetic scope over an active leak doesn't just fail; it manufactures a second failure and a disputed invoice, because the stain reappears through fresh work. Second, the soft floor is also a safety sign, not just a damage sign — Chapter 12 makes that the whole decision. Read water twice: once as damage, once as a warning about where you may stand.

The line to remember: “The stain is the symptom. Somewhere above it, the cause is still dripping.”

The proof — water, held in one line

You seeStains, swelling, soft floors.
It meansWater has been here — possibly still is.
Next jobFind the source before any cosmetic fix.

This row is the programme's damage table, carried whole in Chapter 8. Every kind of damage gets the same three-part treatment: seen, meant, next.

If this is all new to you

Think of a bucket under a dripping tap. You can mop the floor beautifully — and mop it again tomorrow, and the day after. Or you can turn off the tap, and mop once. Water damage works the same way, just slower and hidden inside walls. The source might be a failed roof, a burst pipe, a seal that let weather in. Until the source is found and named, every repair is a mop. After the source, one repair can actually finish the story.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Something lets water in — a roof, a pipe, a seal.
  2. Water travels: down, along beams, into boards and plaster — often far from where it entered.
  3. The signs appear where the water arrived, not where it started.
  4. Fix the arrival point alone, and the water simply writes a new sign beside the fresh paint.

If you've done this work before

This is the chapter where assessors earn their keep in a single sentence on a report: “source not yet found.” Four honest words. They stop a cosmetic scope from being approved against an active leak, they set up the follow-up work truthfully, and they protect the crew that comes next from being blamed for a stain that was always coming back. Teach the class to write those words without embarrassment — an unknown, admitted, is a finding.

The line to remember: “Never treat the ring. Treat what dripped.”

The proof — you'll write this line in Chapter 11

The practice case for water, exactly as the class will meet it later: “Water stain, kitchen ceiling, about two feet across, paint bubbling, source not yet found.” Notice what the line does — it names the damage, the room, the size, and the honest unknown, in one breath. That is identify, document, quantify working before the class has even been taught the words for it.

Chapter 4 · Damage, room two

You smell mold before you see it.

Mold is what grows where dampness sits too long. Dark spots spread across a wall or a corner — and before them, a damp, musty smell that tells you the air itself is wet.

Mold means moisture is still present. Do not just paint over it.

Say it in class

“Paint over mold, and the mold keeps growing underneath the paint — and the house keeps being unhealthy. The moisture must be dealt with first.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Mold announces itself in the doorway, before you're fully in the room: a damp, musty smell, like old wet cloth. Then your eyes catch up — dark spots spreading across a wall, clustering in a corner, creeping along the cold edges where damp collects. Corners and bathrooms are its favourite rooms, because that's where moisture lingers longest. The smell matters as evidence: it tells you the damp isn't a photograph of the past. It's the present tense of the house.

How to read a mold sign, step by step

  1. Notice the smell at the door and say so — it's a finding, not an impression.
  2. Find the spots: which wall, which corner, how far do they spread?
  3. Ask where the moisture is coming from — mold is always water's second act.
  4. Note the safety habit as you go: gloves and eye protection in mold areas, every time (the full safety list is Chapter 11).

If you've done this work before

The professional point: mold is a moisture diagnosis wearing a visible costume. The spots tell you where; the smell tells you it's active. A report that reads “mold present, moisture source not yet identified” is doing real work — it separates the cleaning question from the cause question and stops the file from promising a cure it can't deliver. And keep the health framing plain: the point isn't alarm, it's that a painted-over colony keeps the house unhealthy while looking finished — the worst combination in this trade.

The line to remember: “Mold is not the problem. Mold is the message: moisture lives here.”

The proof — mold, held in one line

You seeDark spots + a damp, musty smell.
It meansMoisture is still present in the house.
Next jobDeal with the moisture first — do not just paint over it.

If this is all new to you

The chapters aren't five separate stories — they're one story told in five rooms. Water arrives first: a leak, a flood, a seal gone. If the water is found and dried, the story can end there. If it sits — in a wall, under a floor, in still air — mold is what grows on it. So when you find mold, you're also reading history: somewhere upstream of those spots, water got in and stayed. The two chapters together teach you to read backwards from the growth to the water, and from the water to the source.

How one becomes the other, step by step

  1. Water enters and isn't dried — a slow leak, a wet season, a sealed-up empty house.
  2. Damp settles into plaster, wood, and still air.
  3. Mold takes hold where the damp sits longest — corners, cold walls, closed rooms.
  4. By the time spots are visible, the moisture problem is older than the spots.

If you've done this work before

This connection is why the damage order in this class is taught as story before skill: a trainee who only memorised “mold = dark spots” will scope a clean. A trainee who understands “mold = moisture still present” will scope the moisture question first and write the report that survives review. Same spots on the wall — completely different file. The chain of reasoning is the product.

The line to remember: “Find mold, and you've found water that never left.”

The proof — you'll write this line in Chapter 11

The practice case for mold: “Dark mold spots, bathroom corner, about three feet of wall, damp smell present.” One corner, about three feet of wall. Notice the smell is written into the report line — in this class, a smell you can describe is evidence, and it belongs on paper next to the measurement.

Chapter 5 · Damage, room three

Some damage is done on purpose.

You walk in and the front door hangs broken. Fixtures — taps, lights, anything that can be unscrewed and carried away — are stripped and gone. Copper pipes are missing from the walls. Graffiti covers a wall.

Vandalism means: secure first, then assess. You do not start assessing a house that is still open to anyone walking in.

Say it in class

“You board it, you lock it — and only then do you look properly. Secure first, then assess.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The other kinds of damage happen to a house. Vandalism is done by someone, and you can read the intent in what's missing. A door hangs broken because someone forced it. Fixtures are stripped because they can be carried and sold. Copper pipes vanish from walls for the same reason — copper is worth money as scrap metal. Graffiti is the signature left behind. When you read a room like this, you're not just listing damage — you're learning that this house has been open, visited, and picked over, and may be visited again tonight.

How to read a vandalism sign, step by step

  1. Start at the entries: which door or window is broken, and is the house open right now?
  2. Inventory what's missing, not just what's broken — fixtures, copper, anything carryable.
  3. Read the walls: graffiti tells you people have had time and privacy inside.
  4. Hold the conclusion the signs point to: this property is a target until it's closed.

If you've done this work before

Theft and damage inside a vacant property is rarely a one-night story — an open, stripped house advertises itself to the next visitor, which is why this chapter's rule is an ordering rule, not a preference. There's also a documentation habit worth teaching here: photograph the entry damage and the missing fixtures as found, before the secure changes the scene. After boarding, nobody can prove what was already gone — the “as found” record is the only thing standing between the file and an argument about when the copper left.

The line to remember: “What's missing tells you as much as what's broken.”

The proof — vandalism, held in one line

You seeBroken entries, stripped fixtures, graffiti.
It meansThe house is open and being visited.
Next jobSecure first, then assess.

If this is all new to you

Assess means look carefully and judge — the skill this whole class is building. But judging takes time inside the property: room by room, photographs, measurements. Doing all that in a house anyone can walk into is backwards twice over. It isn't safe — you don't know who considers this house theirs tonight. And it isn't sound — whatever you carefully record can change the moment you leave, because the door still doesn't close. Board it. Lock it. Then look properly, in a house that will stay the way you left it.

How the order runs, step by step

  1. Arrive and read the entries from outside first.
  2. Secure: board the broken entries, lock what can be locked.
  3. Only now, assess — room by room, as found, with the scene stable.
  4. Report both: the secure you did, and the damage you found inside it.

If you've done this work before

Connect this back to Class 6 for the class: “Secure is the permission slip for every job after it.” There, the line was about locks and lockboxes. Here it's about sequence under pressure — when a property is actively being stripped, every other scope waits behind the secure, including your own assessment. Trainees who internalise ordering rules — permission first, secure first, safety first — stop making the expensive mistakes, because most expensive mistakes in this trade are order mistakes, not effort mistakes.

The line to remember: “Close the house first. Then read it.”

The proof — you'll write this line in Chapter 11

The practice case for vandalism: “Back door broken open, one fixture stripped, graffiti on one wall.” One entry, one fixture, one wall. Notice the line counts what is gone as carefully as what is broken — that habit starts here.

Chapter 6 · Damage, room four

Weather works from the outside in.

Wind, rain, hail, and ice. You see roof marks — shingles torn or missing after wind. Hail dents. Ice damage along the edges, where water froze and forced its way in.

Weather means: check the roof and the envelope before interior work. If the shell is broken, fixing the inside first is wasted work — the next rain comes straight back in.

Say it in class

“The envelope is the house's outer shell — the roof, the walls, the windows, the doors, everything that keeps the outside out. Read the shell before you judge a single room inside it.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Weather damage is read from outside the house, looking at its skin. On the roof: shingles — the overlapping tiles that shed rain — torn away or missing after wind, leaving the layers beneath exposed. Hail leaves dents, little hammer-marks across surfaces. Ice does its work at the edges: water freezes, expands, and forces its way under shingles and into seams, so the damage gathers where the roof meets the wall. Each mark is dated by the storm that made it — the shell remembers every season the house stood empty, and some it stood lived-in, too.

How to read a weather sign, step by step

  1. Walk the outside first: roof lines, edges, gutters, every face the storms hit.
  2. Name the agent: wind, hail, or ice — each leaves a different handwriting.
  3. Then go inside and look for the matching chapter: the ceiling stain under the torn shingles.
  4. Judge the shell's state before judging any interior repair — the shell decides whether interior work can last.

If you've done this work before

The cross-reading in step 3 is the professional move: weather outside and water inside are usually the same event read from two sides of the roof. A trainee who links them writes a report that explains itself. A trainee who doesn't will file “stain, source not yet found” in a house where the source is visible from the street. Teach them to photograph the roofline and the ceiling in the same visit, in that order — the envelope evidence is what turns an honest unknown into a found source on the next file.

The line to remember: “Every ceiling stain has a sky above it. Check the sky's side first.”

The proof — weather, held in one line

You seeRoof, wind and hail marks; ice damage at the edges.
It meansThe shell has been breached — or is about to be.
Next jobCheck roof + envelope before interior work.

If this is all new to you

Picture the house wearing a coat. The envelope is that coat — roof on top, walls around, windows and doors as the zips and buttons. A sealed envelope is why a house can be warm and dry while a storm rages a metre away. Every hole in the envelope — a missing shingle, a cracked seal around a window, a door that no longer closes — is a place where the outside has an invitation in. Reading a house means checking the coat for holes before admiring, or repairing, anything it was supposed to protect.

How the envelope fails, step by step

  1. One element weakens — a shingle lifts, a seal cracks, a door warps.
  2. Weather finds the weakness: wind-driven rain, melting ice, driven snow.
  3. Water enters quietly and becomes Chapter 3's stain, then Chapter 4's mold.
  4. Interior repairs made before the hole closes are repairs made twice.

If you've done this work before

Envelope thinking is also scheduling thinking. It explains why experienced crews sequence a file shell-first even when the order's loudest line item is interior: the order describes work, but the house describes order-of-work. When a trainee can say “envelope first, because the next rain re-enters through the same hole,” they have stopped reading line items and started reading houses — which is the entire ambition of this class.

The line to remember: “Fix the coat before you mend what's inside it.”

The proof — the envelope, as a checklist of four

RoofShingles, edges, flashing — where weather writes largest
WallsCracks, siding, penetrations — the coat's body
WindowsGlass, seals, frames — the usual quiet leaks
DoorsClosure, seals, thresholds — where Chapters 5 and 6 meet
Chapter 7 · Damage, room five

Neglect is damage from nobody caring, for a long time.

The lawn has grown wild. Wood has rotted where rain sat on it. There are pest signs — droppings, nests, holes chewed through wood — because animals moved in when people moved out.

Neglect means long vacancy — and long vacancy means layered damage. Expect to find more than one thing wrong.

Say it in class

“One problem on top of another, each one making the next one worse. In a neglected house, the first thing you find is rarely the only thing there is.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Neglect is the only kind of damage with no event behind it — no storm, no break-in, no burst. Just time, uncared-for. You read it in the lawn gone wild and the beds swallowed by weeds. In wood rotted soft where rain was allowed to sit, season after season, because nobody cleared the gutter or fixed the drip. And in the pest signs: droppings in a corner, a nest in an eave, holes chewed through skirting — animals are honest tenants; they only move in when the human ones have truly left.

How to read a neglect sign, step by step

  1. Read the outside as a clock: how wild is the growth, how deep the leaf litter? That's vacancy, measured in seasons.
  2. Find where water was left sitting — rot maps the spots nobody maintained.
  3. Log the pest signs and where they are; they mark the house's new occupancy.
  4. Set your expectation before you open up the inside: layered damage, plural.

If you've done this work before

Neglect changes your logistics, not just your reading. A long-vacant house eats a schedule: the grass scope hides debris, the debris hides damage, the damage hides more damage. Experienced hands write the first report on a neglected property with deliberately wide eyes — room by room, system by system (Chapter 9) — because the costliest surprise in this trade is the second problem discovered after the first one was already priced. Neglect is the chapter that teaches margin: in attention first, and only then in numbers.

The line to remember: “Neglect is a clock. Learn to read how long she's been alone.”

The proof — neglect, held in one line

You seeOvergrowth, rot, pest signs.
It meansLong vacancy — nobody has cared for a long time.
Next jobExpect layered damage — look for more than one thing wrong.

If this is all new to you

Watch how neglect invites the other four in. The gutter nobody clears overflows — that's water. The water sits in the wall — that's mold. The lawn nobody cuts announces the house is empty — that's vandalism, arriving on schedule. The roof nobody inspects loses its shingles to the next storm — that's weather, walking through a door neglect opened. In a lived-in house, small problems get caught while they're small. In a neglected one, they queue up, layer over layer, and arrive at your clipboard all at once, pretending to be one problem.

How layering happens, step by step

  1. Care stops: no eyes, no small repairs, no one noticing the first drip.
  2. Small problems grow teeth — the drip rots, the crack spreads, the seal fails.
  3. Each grown problem creates the conditions for the next kind of damage.
  4. Months later the house presents as one overwhelming scene — which is really a queue of ordinary problems, stacked.

If you've done this work before

This is the bridge to Chapter 3 of the whole course — vacancy itself is damage — now felt at room scale. It also sets up the assessment discipline of Chapter 11: in a layered house, the temptation is to write one big word (“trashed,” “destroyed”) and move on. The skill refuses that word. Layer by layer, kind by kind, room by room — the stack, named. A layered house read carefully is just five familiar chapters in one binding.

The line to remember: “Don't read the pile. Read the layers.”

The proof — one house, all five kinds at once

Hold this composite in mind for the rest of the course — it's the honest picture of the work: her roof lost shingles two winters ago (weather), the ceiling below it rings brown (water), the bathroom corner smells damp and darkens (mold), the back door hangs open and a fixture is gone (vandalism) — and all of it happened because nobody was there to catch the first shingle (neglect). Five chapters, one house. That's why the next chapter puts them in a single table.

Chapter 8 · The story, on one page

Five kinds. One table. Carry it in your head.

That was the damage story. Here it is whole — every kind, what you see when you walk in, and what it means for the next job. This table is the first half of today, folded small enough to take into any house.

Story first, skill second. The story is done. From here, we practise judging.

DamageWhat you see when you walk inWhat it means for the next job
WaterStains, swelling, soft floorsFind the source before any cosmetic fix
MoldDark spots + damp smellMoisture is still present — do not just paint over it
VandalismBroken entries, stripped fixtures, graffitiSecure first, then assess
WeatherRoof/wind/hail marks, ice damageCheck roof + envelope before interior work
NeglectOvergrowth, rot, pest signsLong vacancy — expect layered damage
Say it in class

“Five columns would fit on an index card. The judgment behind them is the rest of your career. Seen — meant — next. Every kind, every time.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Don't memorise the table as homework — use it as a route. Walk a room and ask the five questions in order: anything wet? Anything growing? Anything broken by hands? Anything the weather got at? Anything time got at? Five questions, room by room, and a house has very few places left to hide. Then, for each kind you found, the third column tells you what it means — so your report doesn't just describe the house, it already points at the right next job.

How a table-walk runs, step by step

  1. Outside first: weather and neglect read from the street.
  2. Entries next: vandalism declares itself at the doors.
  3. Room by room inside: water's signs high and low, mold by nose and eye.
  4. Before you leave, run the five once more from memory — what did the house not show you yet?

If you've done this work before

The table's quiet power is in the third column. Novices write descriptions; professionals write implications. “Stain on ceiling” describes. “Stain on ceiling — source to be found before any cosmetic scope” directs. The table trains the second habit by welding each observation to its consequence, so the file that reaches the office already argues for the right next step. That's half of what “processor judgment” means, taught before the word processor is ever mentioned.

The line to remember: “Describe what you saw. Then write what it means. The second sentence is the job.”

The proof — the table is the programme's own

These five rows are carried exactly as the class schedule holds them — same signs, same meanings, nothing added and nothing softened. Where the course's deeper files keep longer catalogues, this table stays the pocket version: five kinds, three columns, no exceptions smuggled in.

If this is all new to you

A table can name a thing; it cannot measure it. “Water” is a kind. “A stain two feet across in one room, source not yet found” is a finding. The distance between those two sentences is the whole second half of today: the house herself (her systems, her age), then the skill — identify, document, quantify — that turns kinds into findings a file can stand on. Keep the table. Just don't mistake it for the reading.

How the class moves on, step by step

  1. The story half ends here: five kinds, understood.
  2. Chapter 9 steps back: to judge damage, know what the house is made of.
  3. Chapter 10 adds the modifiers: age, region, season, construction.
  4. Chapter 11 turns all of it into the three-step skill, with practice.

If you've done this work before

Worth saying plainly to a class that loves a tidy table: every real dispute you've ever seen on a file — the short-paid invoice, the rejected scope, the “but the photo shows…” argument — happened in the gap between naming and measuring. The table prevents wrong names. Only quantification prevents wrong numbers. Teach both halves with equal reverence and the class will understand why this session is built in two.

The line to remember: “The table names it. The skill measures it. You need both.”

The proof — the session's own architecture

The schedule builds this session in exactly this order and says why on its face: “Story first, skill second — because you cannot judge what you do not understand.” This page keeps that order slide for slide. If a future teacher is tempted to start with the checklist, this drawer is the counter-argument, kept where they'll find it.

Chapter 9 · The house herself

Before you judge damage, know what a house is made of.

A house has five systems, and each one does a job, and each one fails in its own way: the roof, the plumbing, HVAC, the electrical, and the structure.

Damage is what happened. Systems are where it happened — and where it will spread if nobody reads it.

Say it in class

“Five systems. The roof keeps rain out. The plumbing carries water in and waste out. HVAC warms, moves, and cools the air. The electrical carries power. The structure is the skeleton that holds it all up. Learn what each one does, and its failures start introducing themselves.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Take them one at a time. The roof keeps rain out; when it fails, water comes in from above and you see stains on the ceilings below. The plumbing carries water in and waste water out; when it fails, you get leaks, bursts, and damp. HVAC is one word for three jobs — heating, ventilation, and air conditioning; when it fails, the house goes cold, or damp, or airless, and damp is where mold begins. The electrical system carries power; when it fails, lights die and outlets go dead — and damaged wiring near water becomes a hazard, not just a fault. The structure is the skeleton — frame, floors, the walls that hold everything up; when it fails, floors sag, stairs feel unsafe, ceilings bow.

How a systems-walk runs, step by step

  1. Start at the top: roof state, then the ceilings under it.
  2. Follow the water: plumbing runs, fixtures, traps — where it enters, where it leaves.
  3. Feel the air: HVAC — is the house warm, moving, dry? Or cold, still, damp?
  4. Check the power with respect: dead is information; damaged-near-water is danger.
  5. End with the skeleton: floors under your feet, stairs under your hand, ceilings over your head.

If you've done this work before

Systems thinking is what turns five damage kinds into one diagnosis. The ceiling stain (water) stops being a mystery when you hold it against the roof system above it and the plumbing run beside it. The musty corner (mold) reads differently once you ask what the HVAC has been doing — or not doing — for a year. Teach the class to file every damage observation under a system in their notes; a finding with a system attached is a finding with a cause half-found already.

The line to remember: “Name the system, and the damage starts explaining itself.”

The proof — five systems, five failures

RoofKeeps rain out → fails as leaks; signs appear on ceilings below.
PlumbingWater in, waste out → fails as leaks, bursts, damp.
HVACHeat, air movement, cooling → fails as cold, damp, airless rooms.
ElectricalPower through the house → fails as dead outlets — and hazard near water.
StructureThe skeleton → fails as sagging floors, unsafe stairs, bowing ceilings.

If this is all new to you

Systems lean on each other, so failures cascade. A plumbing leak (plumbing) soaks a joist (structure) and feeds a colony (mold). A dead furnace (HVAC) lets pipes freeze and burst (plumbing) in the coldest week of the year — which is exactly why winterization exists. A failing roof (weather's target) becomes water, then rot, then a soft floor your foot finds before your eyes do. When you read a house system by system, you stop being surprised by the second and third problem — you start predicting where they'll be.

How one failure becomes three, step by step

  1. A system fails quietly — a slow leak, a dead furnace, a lifted shingle.
  2. Its neighbour system absorbs the insult: wood drinks water, air stays damp, pipes freeze.
  3. The second failure shows its own signs, in a different room, wearing a different chapter's name.
  4. The reader who knows the systems connects them into one story — and one honest report.

If you've done this work before

This is the intellectual core of the whole session, so land it slowly: assessment quality is prediction quality. Anyone can photograph a stain. The reader the client trusts is the one whose report says, in effect, “given this roof and this winter, also check here, here, and here.” That sentence can only be written by someone holding the systems map. It's also why the frozen-pipe cascade is taught in reverse here: the class met winterization as a procedure in Class 7; today they meet it as a systems argument.

The line to remember: “Damage travels along systems. Read the routes, not just the wreckage.”

The proof — the cascade you'll meet again

One cascade ties three classes together, and it's worth stating plainly: heat fails → pipes freeze → pipes burst → water spreads → floors soften and mold follows. Class 7 taught the procedure that interrupts it. This chapter teaches why the procedure exists. Chapter 12 will ask what you do when you walk into the end of that cascade — and the answer starts with safety, not with a mop.

Chapter 10 · The modifiers

An old house is a different patient.

The typical home lived in by its owner was 42 years old in 2024 — up from 31 in 2005. And about 47 out of every 100 owner-occupied homes were built before 1980. Older houses carry older problems: older pipes, older wiring, older roofs.

Age does not decide the job. It tells you where to look first. Our house, born in the biggest TOTAL building year, is no spring chicken either.

Say it in class

“Read the house before you price the job. Never price a job from a photograph alone and call it understanding. Walk it — or study the walk — and then decide.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Median means the middle: half of homes are older, half are younger. In 2024 the middle owner-occupied home — a home lived in by the person who owns it — was 42 years old. In 2005 that middle home was 31. The whole stock aged eleven years in nineteen, because far more old houses stayed standing than new ones arrived to pull the middle down. And nearly half of those homes — about 47 in every 100 — were built before 1980. Our house, born in 1972, sits right inside that older half, which is why her story keeps rhyming with the real stock's story.

How age steers a reading, step by step

  1. Ask the house's age before you judge a single room.
  2. Age the systems with her: pipes, wiring, and roof layers of a similar vintage.
  3. Expect the era's materials and the era's shortcuts, and look there first.
  4. Let age order your attention — never let it excuse a missed room.

If you've done this work before

Bid accuracy lives here. Two identical-looking scopes price differently on a 1975 house and a 2015 house, because the older house's “simple” jobs keep discovering company. Trainees who learn to ask “how old is she?” before “how much is it?” stop writing the scopes that come back as change orders and arguments. The median figures give them the reason at national scale: this industry does not mostly serve new houses in trouble. It serves old houses, outliving their systems, in trouble.

The line to remember: “Age tells you where to look first — not what you'll find.”

The proof — dates, numbers, and where they came from

42 yearsMedian age of an owner-occupied home, 2024
31 yearsThe same median in 2005 — the stock aged 11 years in 19
~47%Of owner-occupied homes built before 1980

Figures from the U.S. Census Bureau counts behind the programme's research (see Session 3's sourcing, where the same median appears). Teach them as the middle and the share — never as the age of any particular house.

If this is all new to you

Three quiet forces reshape every job. Region: cold places invented winterization, because water freezes; warm, wet seasons invented the grass cycle, because lawns won't stop. Season: the same house in January and the same house in July present different risks, different access, different damage in progress. Construction and layout: how she was built and how her rooms are arranged change what the work costs and how long it takes — a fact no photograph fully tells you. The reader's rule follows from all three: read the house — in her place, in her season, as she was built — before you price the job.

How the modifiers stack, step by step

  1. Place sets the menu: freeze risk here, growth risk there, storm risk somewhere else.
  2. Season sets the clock: what is actively getting worse this month?
  3. Construction sets the effort: access, layout, materials — the shape of the work itself.
  4. Only after all three does a price mean anything honest.

If you've done this work before

“Never price from a photograph alone” deserves its full weight in the room. A photograph flattens season (was this taken before or after the freeze?), hides construction (what's behind that wall finish?), and lies cheerfully about layout. The professional standard this chapter teaches is modest and absolute: walk it, or study the walk — a complete, sequenced, room-by-room record — and then decide. Pricing off a single flattering image is how good crews lose money on honest work.

The line to remember: “Same house, different place, different month — different job.”

The proof — two jobs that prove the rule

WinterizeA job invented by cold places — it exists because water freezes.
Grass cutA job invented by warm, wet seasons — it exists because lawns grow.

Both jobs were taught as procedures in Classes 6 and 7. Here they return as evidence: the work menu itself is written by geography and season.

Chapter 11 · The skill

Identify. Document. Quantify. In that order.

Identify means name what you see — “water stain on the kitchen ceiling,” not “something bad.” Document means prove it: photographs before, during, and after, and words written room by room, exactly as found. Quantify means measure it. A judgment without a number is a guess. A judgment with a number is a case.

And before any of it — safety. Safety before tidy, always. Tidy can wait. Your body cannot be replaced.

Practise on three teaching cases

Three cases, written for this class — synthetic, labelled, no real house behind them. For each one, do the skill in order in your head first: identify it, draft the report line, quantify it. Then tap to check your line against the class's.

Say it in class

“Identify, document, quantify — in that order, and the order never changes. Do not rush to the fix. The fix comes later. Today, the skill is the reading.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Identify: name what you see, precisely enough to point at. Not “damage in the kitchen” — “water stain on the kitchen ceiling.” Document: prove it with photographs — before, during, and after, with date-stamps where the order requires them — and with written words, room by room, exactly as found. A date-stamp is the date printed on the photograph itself, proving when it was taken. Quantify: measure it. How many rooms? How big is the stain? How many cubic yards? Each step depends on the one before: you can't document what you haven't named, and you can't measure what you haven't proven is there.

How one finding travels the three steps

  1. Identify: “Dark spots, bathroom corner.”
  2. Document: photograph the corner wide and close; write it as found, smell included.
  3. Quantify: “About three feet of wall, one corner.”
  4. The report line assembles itself: “Dark mold spots, bathroom corner, about three feet of wall, damp smell present.”

If you've done this work before

Notice how much of the later course is pre-loaded in these three verbs. The Processor's entire craft (Class 9) is document-and-quantify done at a desk: tagging proof to line items, checking honest quantities, refusing to paper over gaps. The Client Manager's payment defence is identify done in writing months earlier. Teach the verbs as a career, not a lesson: the trainee who quantifies honestly today is the one whose invoices survive contact with a reviewer who wasn't there.

The line to remember: “A judgment without a number is a guess. A judgment with a number is a case.”

The proof — the three report lines, word for word

Water“Water stain, kitchen ceiling, about two feet across, paint bubbling, source not yet found.”
Mold“Dark mold spots, bathroom corner, about three feet of wall, damp smell present.”
Vandalism“Back door broken open, one fixture stripped, graffiti on one wall.”

These are the practice exercise's answer lines, kept identical here so the class hears one standard everywhere on the page.

The safety list — all six, in order

  1. Never enter an unsafe structure alone.
  2. Check floors, stairs, and ceilings before walking them.
  3. Treat standing water + electricity as live danger.
  4. Wear gloves and eye protection for debris and mold areas.
  5. Stop and report hazards instead of working through them.
  6. Animals, squatters, or weapons signs = leave and escalate. Squatters are people living in a house without permission. Escalate means hand it upward, to the office, immediately — do not handle it yourself.

If this is all new to you

Picture the walk the list describes: you arrive, you look at the house from outside first, you check the floors before you trust them, you keep your gloves and eye protection on — and the moment something feels unsafe, you stop, you step out, and you report. That is not cowardice. That is the job done right. Every rule on the list protects the same order this whole class teaches: the person first, then the proof, then the work.

If you've done this work before

Worth naming the two rules that get negotiated away in the field, so the class hears them defended in advance. Rule 2 — checking floors before walking them — is the one today's decision turns on: a soft floor is information about your own safety, not a patch of damage to step around. And rule 5 — stop and report — is a complete action, not a pause in the action: the report is the deliverable on the day the house says no.

The line to remember: “Safety before tidy, always.”

How the walk feels when the list is working

Slow at the door. Eyes up, then down. Gloves on before the first debris room, not after the first sharp edge. And a standing permission, granted in this classroom, that no schedule outranks: when a house feels wrong, leaving and reporting is the completed task. The next chapter's decision is built entirely out of this list — a stained ceiling, a soft floor, a broken door, and six rules that already know the answer.

Chapter 12 · The decision, and the close

Stain, soft floor, broken door. What first?

One last look at our house. The ceiling is stained. A floor is soft underfoot. A back door hangs broken open. Three things shout at you at once: the house is unsafe, the damage needs proving, and the work needs doing.

What does this house need first — safety, proof, or work? And what is the very first action you take?

Make the call

Pairs first — thirty seconds, one answer, a reason ready. Then tap your verdict and check it against the expert reveal. Reasoning is what's graded here; the reveal explains the order either way.

Say it in class

“Safety first, then proof, then work.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The order is safety, then proof, then work — in that order, always. And the first action is not heroic: make it safe. Do not walk the soft floor. Do not work in a house with a broken-open door. Secure the entry, step back, and report the hazard. Then prove what you found, with photographs and a written report. Then, and only then, the work begins. Anyone who jumps to work before safety has the order backwards — and backwards in this business gets people hurt.

How the decision runs, step by step

  1. Three shouts compete: unsafe, unproven, undone. Rank them by what can't be undone — an injury can't.
  2. Safety: secure the entry, keep off the soft floor, report the hazard.
  3. Proof: photograph and write the house as found — stain, floor, door, each identified, documented, quantified.
  4. Work: only now, scoped from the proof, in the order the proof demands.

If you've done this work before

Notice that the reveal dignifies all three instincts before ranking them. The trainee who said “proof” was protecting the file; the one who said “work” was protecting the house. Both instincts are assets in this trade — they're just out of order for the first hour. The teacher's move is to praise the instinct and correct the sequence, because sequence is teachable and instinct is not. That's the rubric for the whole session in one gesture: reasoning praised, guessing corrected, order non-negotiable.

The line to remember: “Safety, then proof, then work.”

The proof — every chapter of today, inside one doorway

Check the composite against the course: the stain is Chapter 3 (water — source not yet found). The damp that surely follows is Chapter 4. The broken door is Chapter 5 — and its rule, secure first, is literally step one of the reveal. The soft floor is Chapter 9's structure, failing. That all four are present at once is Chapter 7: layered damage, in a house time forgot. Today's decision isn't a new lesson — it's the whole session, standing in one doorway, asking to be read in the right order.

If this is all new to you

Before you leave: one line each, in your own words. What does this house need first, and why? Say it in one line. If you can say it in one line, you know it — and what you know, you can do, on any house, in any town, on any day. That's the promise of the whole class: the house changes, the street changes, the order she arrives on changes — the reading doesn't.

How to run the close, step by step

  1. Go around the room — one line each, no notes, no repeats of the last person's wording.
  2. Listen for the order inside each line: safety named before proof, proof before work.
  3. Anyone whose line inverts the order gets one warm retry, not a correction speech.
  4. End on the anchor, said together: safety, then proof, then work.

If you've done this work before

And here's where it leads, so the class leaves facing forward: they can read a house now. Next, they follow the money — where it leaks between a bid and a payment, who owns each leak, and the three people who carry one file from order to cash. Every number in that class will trace back to a reading made in this one: an identified, documented, quantified finding is the only kind a bid can be built on. The reading was never separate from the money. It was the money, upstream.

The line to remember: “What you know, you can do — on any house, in any town, on any day.”

The proof — what the class carries out the door

5 kindsWater, mold, vandalism, weather, neglect — seen, meant, next
5 systemsRoof, plumbing, HVAC, electrical, structure
3 verbsIdentify, document, quantify — in that order
1 orderSafety, then proof, then work — always
Tip: use the ← and → keys to move between chapters — and open the full notes on any slide to re-learn the topic from scratch

All 12 slides

The full arc of Class 8 on one screen — retrieval, the five kinds of damage, the five systems, the skill, and the decision. Tap any slide to jump to it.

The logic behind this page

Why Class 8 is built the way it is — story before skill, a table in the middle, safety wrapped around the whole thing — and what its numbers do, and don't, prove. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

Story first, skill second — on purpose

The schedule builds this session in two halves and defends the order on its face: first the damage story (what happens to a house), then the damage skill (how you assess it) — “because you cannot judge what you do not understand.” This page keeps that architecture slide for slide. Chapters 3–7 are pure story: five kinds of damage, each with its signs and its consequence. The skill — identify, document, quantify — does not appear until Chapter 11, when the class has something worth applying it to. A version of this class that opened with the checklist would be shorter, tidier, and worse: trainees would perform the verbs on houses they cannot yet see.

Why the table sits in the middle

  • The table is the hinge, not the summary. Placed at Chapter 8, it folds the story half small enough to carry — and its own second drawer states its limit out loud: a table can name a thing; it cannot measure it. That honesty is what makes the skill half feel necessary rather than decorative.
  • Every kind gets the same three beats. Seen — meant — next. Water, mold, vandalism, weather, neglect are each taught as observation, implication, consequence. The repetition is the training: by the fifth kind, the class is predicting the third column before it appears.
  • Layered damage is the truth-teller. Chapter 7 admits what the tidy chapters imply away: real houses present with several kinds at once, stacked by time. The decision slide then grades exactly that — a composite house, read in the right order.

Why safety wraps the skill instead of following it

  • The six safety rules are printed in full, once, in Chapter 11's second drawer — never summarised into a slogan on the slide face. “Safety before tidy” is the memory hook; the list is the content. Both are needed: the hook for the doorway moment, the list for everything after it.
  • The decision is the anchor. Class 1 anchored on a name, Class 2 on a drawn loop. Class 8 anchors on an order — safety, then proof, then work — rehearsed in the exercise, defended in the drawer, and spoken together at the close. If the class keeps one thing, it is that sequence.
  • The practice cases are words, not photographs, deliberately: the schedule's cases are synthetic and labelled, and this page practises the report line — the judgement artefact — rather than faking photo evidence. The three answer lines are identical in the exercise, the drawer, and the schedule, so the class hears one standard everywhere.

What isn't proven — the open questions, honestly

  • The age figures (median 42 in 2024, 31 in 2005, ~47% built before 1980) are population statistics about the national stock. They steer attention; they say nothing certain about any individual house, and the page teaches them that way.
  • The five-kind table and the five-system map are the programme's working framework — a field lens, not a taxonomy from a standards body. Finer catalogues exist in the deeper files; this page keeps the pocket version and says so.
  • Nothing here prices a repair. “Read the house before you price the job” is a sequencing rule, not a rate card — rates come from the governing rulebook on the order, and this page invents none.
  • Mold is taught at recognition level only: signs, meaning, and the moisture-first rule. Remediation methods, testing, and health thresholds are outside this session and are not improvised on the page.
  • The three practice cases are teaching composites written for this class. Any resemblance to a real property is the resemblance of all vacant houses to each other.

Running the class from this page

  • Open cold, calculator warm. Slide 1 tests two memories at once — winterization recited, CY maths computed. The calculator is live so a dispute about 9 × 6 × 3 settles in seconds, without the teacher becoming the answer key.
  • Walk the five rooms at story pace. Resist summarising a kind before its chapter. Each one's third beat — what it means for the next job — is where the class should slow down; that column is the session's real syllabus.
  • Protect the decision. If time runs short, cut discussion elsewhere — never the Chapter 12 verdict and the one-line close. The order is the anchor the next class opens from.
  • This page is the spine, not a guest. If a live Muse segment joins the class, it belongs in the Muse app, projected, in one short mid-class slot — and this page can still carry the whole lesson if the connection ever fails.
  • Nothing here is real client data — the house is a teaching character, the cases are labelled composites, and every rule is taught as the programme teaches it: typical — always check the order.

Where it all came from

Every number on the slides names its home in its drawer. In short:

  • House-age figures (median owner-occupied age 42 in 2024 and 31 in 2005; ~47% built before 1980): the U.S. Census Bureau counts carried in the programme's research, where the same figures anchor Session 3.
  • The five damage kinds, their signs and consequences, the five house systems, the identify–document–quantify skill, the six safety rules, the three practice cases and their report lines, and the closing decision: Session 8 of the programme's class schedule and blueprint, carried whole — story, skill, decision, and the exact closing line, “Safety first, then proof, then work.”
  • Winterization steps and the cubic-yard arithmetic (9 × 6 × 3 = 162 cu ft ÷ 27 = 6 CY): Session 7, retrieved here from memory as the schedule directs.

This is the demo version of Class 8 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property, and the practice cases are labelled teaching composites. Everything here is a teaching example — no real clients, work orders, or company details anywhere on the page.
